headline: Medium risk: shared customer-support workflows create prompt-injection, leakage, and output-cascade paths; no direct pairwise evidence is documented.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Agent A can ingest files, browser content, and runtime-injected MCPs/hooks; agent B is a customer-support bot that exchanges messages over Slack/Messenger-style channels. That creates a plausible path where A’s untrusted content reaches B as instructions. The pair lacks direct interaction docs, so uncertainty is resolved upward.
conditions: IF agent_a forwards browser/file content into a shared chat channel used by agent_b
IF agent_b parses inbound messages as instructions without provenance checks
mitigations: Disable automatic forwarding from A to B
Add provenance tags to all A-originated messages
Require B to treat A output as untrusted text
Restrict A’s browser/file ingestion to allowlisted sources
requires-engineering: add message-signing or provenance enforcement

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches session history, project code, AGENTS.md/README.md, and provider auth prompts; agent B handles text/voice over external messaging APIs. If they share a workspace or hand off transcripts, sensitive context from A can leak into B’s outbound channels. No direct shared-storage evidence exists, so the safer choice is medium rather than low.
conditions: IF agent_a and agent_b share a workspace or transcript store
IF A-originated content includes provider auth prompts or session history and B relays it externally
mitigations: Separate workspaces for A and B
Redact auth prompts before any handoff
Disable transcript export from shared channels
Limit B to non-sensitive text classes
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: A has broad network egress, browser execution, subprocesses, and multiple-instance support; B has allowlisted egress and no multiple-instance support. Their capabilities overlap on outbound communication and mutable conversation state, so concurrent use can conflict on shared resources or rate limits. The profiles do not prove a shared lock, so uncertainty escalates to medium.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same external channel or queue
IF the orchestrator schedules concurrent sessions against a shared mutable resource
mitigations: Serialize writes to shared channels
Assign disjoint API credentials
Throttle A’s subprocess-driven retries
Run B in a single-worker queue
requires-engineering: add distributed locking

D_cascading_error.rationale: A can generate browser-sourced or tool-mediated content, and B is a dialogue agent that can act on inbound text. If B treats A’s output as authoritative, errors or fabricated facts can cascade into customer-facing responses. Because no verification layer is documented between them, the safer severity is high.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output without independent verification
IF A’s browser-derived content is used as customer-facing guidance
mitigations: Insert a human review step before B replies
Require citations or source links from A
Block A outputs lacking confidence metadata
Constrain B to template-based responses
requires-engineering: add automated fact-checking

E_compliance.rationale: A handles provider auth prompts, installation identifiers, session history, and project code; B handles text/voice through third-party messaging platforms. That combination can create retention and residency mismatches if the same customer data is routed through both systems. No specific jurisdictional mismatch is documented, so medium is the appropriate conservative level.
conditions: IF regulated customer data is routed through both agents
IF retention or deletion policies differ between A’s local artifacts and B’s messaging backends
mitigations: Exclude regulated data from the pair
Document retention for each channel
Purge A session history after use
Use region-appropriate messaging endpoints
requires-engineering: align retention and residency controls
